3. Reverse engineering my Coway air purifier to ditch the cloud

Source: HackerNews | Topic: hn | Coverage: 1 source | Discussion

Summary

A developer reverse-engineered their Coway air purifier to remove its dependency on cloud-based servers. By modifying the device's firmware and communication protocols, the user gained local control over the hardware. This project highlights the growing trend of users reclaiming ownership of their IoT devices.

My Take

Why let a perfectly good air purifier phone home to a server in another hemisphere just to tell you the air is clean? It’s peak modern absurdity that we have to hack our own appliances just to stop them from being glorified data-mining spies. If you don't own the firmware, you don't really own the device; you're just renting a paperweight with an internet connection.

4. Jonathan Blow – If AI solved coding, why is my software still the same? [video]

Source: HackerNews | Topic: hn | Coverage: 1 source | Discussion

Summary

Jonathan Blow discusses the discrepancy between the hype surrounding AI-assisted coding and the lack of tangible improvement in software quality. He argues that despite the integration of AI tools, software remains as buggy and inefficient as ever. The video questions the actual utility of current generative AI in professional software engineering.

My Take

AI is currently the world’s most expensive autocomplete, and we’re all acting like it’s the second coming of Alan Turing. It’s great at writing boilerplate code that nobody wants to read, but it still can't fix the fundamental problem that software is hard and humans are messy. Don't confuse the speed of writing code with the quality of the product; shipping faster just means you're delivering bugs at a higher velocity.

My Take
